name: Collection Framework

beginner.content:
What is Collection Framework?

A Collection Framework is a unified architecture that provides a set of classes and interfaces to store, manipulate, and retrieve groups of objects efficiently. In simple terms: Framework = Classes + Interfaces.

Why Do We Need Collections?

In Java, arrays have several limitations:

  • Fixed Size - Once an array is created, its size cannot be changed. You must know the size in advance, which can lead to wasted memory or insufficient space.
  • Homogeneous - Arrays can only store elements of the same data type. You cannot mix different types in a single array.
  • No Readymade Methods - Arrays do not provide built-in methods for common operations like sorting, searching, or removing elements.

Differences Between Array and Collection


  • Size: Arrays are fixed size; Collections are growable (dynamic size).
  • Data Types: Arrays are homogeneous; Collections can hold heterogeneous objects.
  • Methods: Arrays have no readymade methods; Collections provide readymade methods (add, remove, contains, sort, etc.).
  • Primitives: Arrays can hold primitives; Collections can only hold objects (use wrapper classes for primitives).
  • Memory: Arrays may waste memory; Collections manage memory dynamically.

Collection Hierarchy

The Collection Framework has a well-defined hierarchy:

  • Iterable(I) - Root interface
  • Collection(I) - Extends Iterable
    • List(I) - Ordered, allows duplicates (ArrayList, LinkedList, Vector, Stack)
    • Set(I) - Unordered, no duplicates (HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet)
    • Queue(I) - FIFO ordering (PriorityQueue, Deque)

  • Map(I) - Separate hierarchy, key-value pairs (HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, Hashtable)

The 9 Key Interfaces of the Collection Framework

The framework is built around 9 core interfaces: Collection, List, Set, SortedSet, NavigableSet, Queue, Map, SortedMap, and NavigableMap.

  • Collection is considered the root interface of the framework - it defines the most common methods applicable to any collection object (add, remove, size, etc.).
  • There is no concrete class that implements the Collection interface directly - you always work through one of its child interfaces (List, Set, Queue) and their implementing classes.

Collection Framework Hierarchy at a Glance

A clean side-by-side view of every interface, its key implementing classes, and its defining behavior:

InterfaceExtendsImplementing ClassesOrderDuplicates
ListCollectionArrayList, LinkedList, Vector, StackInsertion orderAllowed
SetCollectionHashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSetNo / insertion / sortedNot allowed
QueueCollectionPriorityQueue, ArrayDeque, LinkedListFIFO (or priority)Allowed
DequeQueueArrayDeque, LinkedListBoth endsAllowed
Map(none - separate hierarchy)HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, HashtableDepends on impl.Keys unique, values may repeat

Note: Map is deliberately NOT part of the Collection interface hierarchy - it stores key-value pairs rather than single elements, so its method contract (put/get by key) is fundamentally different from add/remove used by List, Set, and Queue.

Iterable and Collection Interfaces

The Iterable interface is the root of the collection hierarchy. Any class that implements Iterable can be used with the enhanced for-each loop. It provides the iterator() method.

Collection Interface Methods

The Collection interface extends Iterable and defines the most common operations for all collections:

  • add(Object o) - Adds an element to the collection
  • addAll(Collection c) - Adds all elements from another collection
  • remove(Object o) - Removes a single instance of the specified element
  • removeAll(Collection c) - Removes all elements that are in the specified collection
  • retainAll(Collection c) - Retains only elements that are in the specified collection
  • clear() - Removes all elements from the collection
  • contains(Object o) - Returns true if the collection contains the element
  • containsAll(Collection c) - Returns true if the collection contains all elements of the specified collection
  • isEmpty() - Returns true if the collection is empty
  • size() - Returns the number of elements
  • toArray() - Converts the collection to an array
  • iterator() - Returns an Iterator over the elements

List Interface Specifics

The List interface extends Collection and represents an ordered collection (sequence). Key characteristics:

  • Ordered - Elements maintain their insertion order
  • Allows Duplicates - Same element can appear multiple times
  • Index-Based Access - Elements can be accessed by their integer index

Additional List Methods

  • get(int index) - Returns element at specified index
  • set(int index, Object o) - Replaces element at specified index
  • indexOf(Object o) - Returns first occurrence index, or -1
  • lastIndexOf(Object o) - Returns last occurrence index, or -1
  • listIterator() - Returns a ListIterator for bidirectional traversal
  • subList(int from, int to) - Returns a view of the portion between from (inclusive) and to (exclusive)

Queue and Deque Interfaces

The Queue interface extends Collection and represents a collection designed for holding elements prior to processing, typically in FIFO (First-In-First-Out) order.

Key Queue Methods (Pairs That Behave Differently on Failure)


OperationThrows ExceptionReturns Special Value
Insertadd(e)offer(e)
Removeremove()poll()
Examineelement()peek()

Deque (Double-Ended Queue)

Deque extends Queue and allows insertion/removal from both ends - front and rear. It can be used as both a Queue (FIFO) and a Stack (LIFO). ArrayDeque is the recommended, faster, non-synchronized replacement for the legacy Stack class.

  • addFirst(e) / addLast(e) - Insert at front / rear
  • removeFirst() / removeLast() - Remove from front / rear
  • peekFirst() / peekLast() - Examine front / rear without removing
  • push(e) / pop() - Stack-style operations (both act on the front)

Iterator vs ListIterator

Java provides different cursor types for traversing collections. Understanding their differences is critical for advanced usage.

Iterator

  • Can traverse any Collection (List, Set, Queue)
  • Supports only forward direction traversal
  • Methods: hasNext(), next(), remove()
  • Obtained via collection.iterator()

ListIterator

  • Can only traverse List objects
  • Supports bidirectional traversal (forward and backward)
  • Methods: hasNext(), next(), hasPrevious(), previous(), nextIndex(), previousIndex(), remove(), set(), add()
  • Obtained via list.listIterator()

Cursor Types in Java


  • Enumeration - Legacy cursor for Vector. Methods: hasMoreElements(), nextElement(). Read-only, forward-only.
  • Iterator - Universal cursor for any Collection. Forward-only. Supports remove operation.
  • ListIterator - Most powerful cursor but only for Lists. Bidirectional. Supports add, set, and remove.

Fail-Fast vs Fail-Safe Iterators


  • Fail-Fast Iterators: Immediately throw ConcurrentModificationException if the collection is structurally modified after the iterator is created (except through the iterator's own methods). Examples: iterators of ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet. They work on the original collection.
  • Fail-Safe Iterators: Do NOT throw ConcurrentModificationException. CopyOnWriteArrayList iterates a frozen snapshot taken when the iterator was created, so later changes are invisible to it. ConcurrentHashMap is different: its iterators are weakly consistent - they traverse the live table and MAY reflect updates made after creation, they simply never throw.

Collection Interface vs Collections Utility Class

One of the most common points of confusion for beginners: Collection (singular, an interface) and Collections (plural, a final utility class) are two completely different things that just happen to share a similar name.

Collection (interface)Collections (class)
Root interface of the frameworkfinal utility class in java.util
Defines instance methods like add(), remove()Provides only static helper methods
Implemented by ArrayList, HashSet, etc.Operates ON a collection passed as an argument
Represents an actual group of objectsCannot be instantiated (private constructor)

Commonly Used Collections Utility Methods


  • Collections.sort(list) - Sorts in natural order (or with a Comparator)
  • Collections.reverse(list) - Reverses the order of elements
  • Collections.shuffle(list) - Randomly shuffles elements
  • Collections.max(coll) / Collections.min(coll) - Finds the largest/smallest element
  • Collections.unmodifiableList(list) - Returns a read-only view of the list
  • Collections.synchronizedList(list) - Returns a thread-safe wrapper
  • Collections.emptyList() / emptySet() / emptyMap() - Returns an immutable empty collection
  • Collections.frequency(coll, obj) - Counts how many times an element occurs

Choosing the Right Collection

A quick decision guide for picking the correct collection type based on the requirement:

RequirementBest ChoiceWhy
Fast random access by indexArrayListBacked by array, O(1) get()
Frequent insert/delete in the middleLinkedListO(1) relink once you hold the node - but add(int,E)/remove(int) must traverse first, so the whole operation is O(n)
Thread-safe listVector or Collections.synchronizedList()Synchronized access
LIFO stack behaviorArrayDeque (preferred over Stack)Faster, not synchronized, purpose-built
No duplicates, order doesn't matterHashSetO(1) add/contains
No duplicates, preserve insertion orderLinkedHashSetHash table + linked list
No duplicates, need sorted orderTreeSetRed-Black tree, always sorted
Key-value lookup, order doesn't matterHashMapO(1) average get/put
Key-value lookup, sorted by keyTreeMapRed-Black tree, sorted keys
FIFO processing / task queueArrayDeque or LinkedListImplements Queue naturally
Process by priority, not insertion orderPriorityQueueMin-heap, orders by natural/Comparator order
Thread-safe Map for concurrent accessConcurrentHashMapSegment-level locking, high concurrency

Fresher Notes

  • The Collections Framework is a set of interfaces and classes in java.util for storing and processing groups of objects.
  • Main interfaces: List (ordered, duplicates), Set (unique), Queue/Deque, and Map (key-value, not a Collection).
  • Code to the interface: List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The framework has two roots: Collection (List, Set, Queue) and Map. Abstract skeletons (AbstractList, AbstractMap) provide partial implementations. Iterable lets any collection work in the for-each loop. Since Java 21, SequencedCollection adds first, last and reversed views to ordered types.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Choose by access pattern. Streams give a declarative pipeline over collections: filter, map, collect, groupingBy. Factory methods List.of, Set.of and Map.of return immutable collections that reject nulls. Arrays.asList is a fixed-size view over an array.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Pick by need: ArrayList for fast index access, LinkedList for queue/deque use, HashSet for uniqueness, TreeSet/TreeMap for sorted data, HashMap for lookups.
  • The Collections utility class gives sort, reverse, shuffle, unmodifiableList and synchronizedList.
  • Use List.of, Set.of, Map.of for small immutable collections (Java 9+).

Senior Notes

  • Know complexity: ArrayList get O(1), add amortized O(1); HashMap get O(1) average; TreeMap O(log n).
  • Fail-fast iterators throw ConcurrentModificationException when a collection is changed during iteration; concurrent collections are weakly consistent.
  • Prefer immutable collections and defensive copies at API boundaries; use concurrent collections (ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList) for threads.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: modifying a collection while iterating, using mutable objects as keys, using raw types, relying on HashSet or HashMap order, using Vector or Hashtable in new code, and returning internal mutable collections from getters (breaks encapsulation). Return copies or unmodifiable views.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance depends on choice: ArrayList iteration is cache friendly, HashMap with a good hash is O(1), and boxing costs memory (an Integer list uses much more than int[]). For primitives consider arrays, IntStream or libraries like fastutil or Eclipse Collections. Measure with JMH before optimizing.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an LRU cache built on LinkedHashMap, a word counter with HashMap.merge, and a unique sorted tag list with TreeSet.

ArrayList - Core Points

  • The ArrayList (C) extends the AbstractList (C) & implements the List interface (I).
  • It uses a Dynamic Array to store duplicate elements of different data types.
  • It is like an array, but there is no size limit. We can add or remove elements anytime. So, it is much more flexible than the traditional array.
  • It is found in the java.util package.
  • Duplicate Element => Allowed.
  • It maintains the insertion order. (Insertion order => preserved / maintain)
  • It is non-synchronized so no thread safety.
  • Heterogeneous Objects => Allowed.
  • Null insertion => Possible. (we can add n number of null values in arraylist)
  • The elements stored in the ArrayList (C) can be randomly accessed, because array works at the index basis.

We can't create an ArrayList of the primitive types, such as int, float, char, etc. It is required to use the required wrapper class in such cases.

ArrayList

ArrayList is a class that extends AbstractList and implements the List interface. It is found in the java.util package. Internally, ArrayList uses a dynamic array (resizable array) to store elements, so there is no fixed size limit.

Key Features of ArrayList


  • Duplicates Allowed - You can add the same element multiple times.
  • Insertion Order Maintained - Elements are stored in the order they are inserted.
  • Non-Synchronized - ArrayList is not thread-safe by default. Multiple threads can access it simultaneously.
  • Heterogeneous Objects Allowed - Without generics, you can store objects of different types.
  • Null Insertion Possible - You can add null values to an ArrayList.
  • Random Access - ArrayList implements the RandomAccess interface, making get operations very fast (O(1)).
  • Best for Retrieval - Due to index-based access, retrieval is very efficient.

Advantages of ArrayList


  • Easy to learn and use
  • Reduces programming effort
  • Increases program speed and quality
  • Faster software reuse

More Built-in ArrayList Methods

Beyond add/get/set/remove, ArrayList provides several other ready-made methods worth knowing:

  • clone() - Creates a shallow copy of the ArrayList.
  • ensureCapacity(int) - Increases the internal array's capacity ahead of time, to avoid repeated resizing.
  • trimToSize() - Shrinks the internal array's capacity down to match the current number of elements.
  • sort() / Collections.sort() - Sorts the list (natural order, or with a custom Comparator).
  • subList(from, to) - Returns a view of a portion of the list between the given indices.
  • toArray() - Converts the ArrayList into an array.
  • addAll() - Appends all elements from another collection.
  • Collections.synchronizedList() - Wraps a (non-thread-safe) ArrayList to get a thread-safe/synchronized view of it.

ArrayList Methods: removeIf(), replaceAll(), retainAll(), forEach()

These functional-style methods (added in Java 8) let you update or filter an ArrayList without writing an explicit loop.

  • removeIf(Predicate) - Removes all elements matching the given condition.
  • replaceAll(UnaryOperator) - Replaces every element with the result of applying the given operation.
  • retainAll(Collection) - Keeps only the elements that are also present in the given collection.
  • forEach(Consumer) - Performs the given action for each element (lambda or method reference).
  • lastIndexOf(Object) - Returns the index of the last occurrence of the element.
  • listIterator() - Like iterator(), but can also move backward using hasPrevious()/previous().

ArrayList: isEmpty(), clear(), removeAll()


  • isEmpty() - Returns true if the ArrayList has no elements.
  • clear() - Removes all elements from the ArrayList, leaving it empty.
  • removeAll(Collection) - Removes from the ArrayList all elements that are also contained in the given collection (passing itself empties the whole list).

Constructor

There are 3 types of constructor as below.

1. ArrayList al = new ArrayList();
ArrayList(): It is used to build an empty array list. Create the empty array list with default initial capacity 10. Once array list reaches its max capacity then new array list will be created with its new capacity.
New Capacity = Current Capacity + (Current Capacity >> 1) - exactly 1.5x, so 10 grows to 15. (The old + 1 form was the Java 6 formula.)

2. ArrayList al = new ArrayList(int initial_capacity);
ArrayList(int capacity): It is used to build an array list that has the specified initial capacity. Here we are passing the int type value.

3. ArrayList al = new ArrayList(Collection c);
ArrayList(Collection<? extends E> c): It is used to build an array list that is initialized with the elements of the collection c. Here we are passing the objects.

ArrayList is the Best Choice if our frequent operation is Retrieval Operation: It implements the random access interface.
ArrayList is the Worst Choice if our frequent operation is Insertion or Deletion (because several shift operations are required for this).

ArrayList Constructors and Internal Working


  • ArrayList(C) extends AbstractList(C) & implements List interface(I).
  • Uses Dynamic Array to Store Duplicate elements of different data types.

Constructors


  • Constructor 1: ArrayList list = new ArrayList(); - Creates an empty ArrayList object with default initial capacity of 10. New Capacity = Current Capacity + (Current Capacity >> 1), so 10 grows to 15.
  • Constructor 2: ArrayList list = new ArrayList(int initialCapacity); - Creates an empty ArrayList object with the given initial capacity.
  • Constructor 3: ArrayList list = new ArrayList(Collection c); - Creates an equivalent ArrayList object for the given collection.

Important Notes


  • We can't create an ArrayList of primitive types (int, float, char). We must use wrapper classes (Integer, Float, Character).
  • Manipulation is slower than LinkedList because a lot of shifting needs to occur when removing elements from the middle.

There are 3 ways to iterate over an ArrayList: Using Simple Way, Using Iterator() Method, and Using For Each Loop.

ArrayList can store heterogeneous objects (different data types) when using ArrayList<Object>. It also allows duplicate elements and null values.

ArrayList of User-Defined Objects


Just like built-in types, an ArrayList can store instances of your own custom classes. This is one of the most common real-world uses of ArrayList - for example, storing a list of Employee, Student, or Product objects.

Getting a Synchronized (Thread-Safe) ArrayList


By default, all ArrayList methods are non-synchronized, so it is not thread-safe. To get a synchronized version, wrap it using Collections.synchronizedList(). When iterating a synchronized list, always wrap the iteration in a synchronized block on the same list to avoid ConcurrentModificationException from concurrent structural changes.

ArrayList spliterator() Method


spliterator() (JDK 8+) splits an ArrayList into parts that can be traversed or processed independently - useful for parallel processing. trySplit() divides the elements into two halves, and tryAdvance() walks through the elements of a spliterator one at a time.

Returning an ArrayList from a Method


A common pattern is to build and populate an ArrayList inside a method, then return it to the caller - useful for encapsulating data-fetching logic (e.g., getting a list of employees from a service layer).

addAll() can be used to copy/merge all the elements of one ArrayList into another existing ArrayList.

Instead of copying into an existing list, you can also merge two ArrayLists into a brand new third one using addAll() twice.

Creating a List with Arrays.asList()


Arrays.asList() (available since JDK 1.2; only List.of() is a Java 9 addition) is a quick way to create a fixed-size List directly from given values, without repeated add() calls. It's commonly combined with subList() to extract a portion of the list.

Interview Questions on ArrayList

  • What is an ArrayList in Java? - ArrayList is a resizable array implementation in the java.util package. It provides dynamic arrays that can grow as needed.
  • How do you create an ArrayList? - ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
  • What are the main differences between ArrayList and LinkedList? - ArrayList uses a dynamic array internally and is best for retrieval, while LinkedList uses a doubly linked list and is best for insertion/deletion operations.
  • How to add elements to an ArrayList? - Using add() to append at the end, or add(index, element) to insert at a specific position.
  • How to remove elements from an ArrayList? - Using remove(index) to remove by position, or remove(Object) to remove by value.
  • How to iterate over an ArrayList? - Using for loop, for-each loop, or Iterator.

ArrayList stores elements in an Object[] elementData plus a size. Default capacity is 10 (allocated lazily on first add). When full, grow allocates oldCapacity + oldCapacity/2 and copies with Arrays.copyOf. modCount increments on structural changes, and iterators compare it to detect concurrent modification (fail-fast).

Mid-Level Notes

  • Inserting or removing in the middle shifts elements, so it is O(n); adding at the end is amortized O(1).
  • When it is full, it grows by about 50% (new array, copy).
  • remove(int index) vs remove(Object o) confuses with Integer lists: use remove(Integer.valueOf(5)).

Senior Notes

  • Pre-size with new ArrayList<>(n) or ensureCapacity to avoid repeated copying.
  • Not thread-safe; use CopyOnWriteArrayList or synchronize externally. subList is a view that breaks if the parent is modified structurally.
  • Iterate with enhanced for or an iterator; remove during iteration with Iterator.remove() or removeIf.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: removing by index vs object on Integer lists, modifying inside for-each, holding a subList after changing the parent, memory leaks (a large ArrayList that is cleared keeps its capacity: use trimToSize or new list), and using ArrayList for frequent inserts at the front.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: add at the end is amortized O(1), add(0, x) is O(n) shifting, contains is O(n). Pre-size to avoid regrowth, prefer removeIf (single pass) over repeated remove (O(n) each), and use ArrayDeque for queue behavior.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: paginating results. Keep a list of items from a query, expose copies of subList ranges and never expose the internal list.

LinkedList

LinkedList is a class that implements the Collection and List interfaces. It is present in the java.util package. Internally, LinkedList uses a doubly linked list structure, where each element (node) contains the data, a reference to the next node, and a reference to the previous node.

Key Features of LinkedList


  • Duplicates Allowed - Same element can be added multiple times.
  • Insertion Order Preserved - Elements maintain the order in which they are inserted.
  • Non-Synchronized - Not thread-safe by default.
  • Heterogeneous Objects Allowed - Can store different types of objects (without generics).
  • Null Insertion Possible - Null values can be added.
  • Best for Insertion/Deletion - Adding or removing elements is very efficient as only pointers need to change.
  • Worst for Retrieval - Accessing elements by index requires traversing the list from the beginning or end (O(n)).
  • Implements Serializable & Cloneable - But does NOT implement the RandomAccess interface (unlike ArrayList), which is why index-based access is slow.

LinkedList Implements List, Deque, and Queue

Unlike ArrayList and Vector (which only implement List), LinkedList uniquely implements three interfaces at once - this is what lets the same class behave as a list, a queue, or a double-ended queue.

InterfaceWhat It Gives LinkedListExample Methods
ListIndex-based, ordered accessget(i), set(i, e), add(i, e)
DequeInsert/remove from both endsaddFirst(), addLast(), pollFirst(), pollLast()
QueueFIFO-style processingoffer(), poll(), peek()

Because it implements Deque, LinkedList can also be used as a Stack (LIFO, via push()/pop()) or a Queue (FIFO, via offer()/poll()) - no separate class needed.

Iteration Methods


There are multiple ways to iterate a LinkedList:

  • 1st Way: Simple Way - Directly print the LinkedList object using System.out.println().
  • 2nd Way: Iterator - Use the iterator() method to get an Iterator and traverse using hasNext() and next().
  • 3rd Way: For Each Loop - Use the enhanced for-each loop to iterate over elements.

Using LinkedList as a Stack and as a Queue

Because LinkedList implements Deque, the same object can be driven with stack-style methods (push/pop) or queue-style methods (offer/poll) - no need for a separate Stack or Queue class.

Interview Questions on LinkedList


1. What is a LinkedList in Java?
A LinkedList is a linear data structure where each element is a separate object called a node. Each node contains data and a reference (link) to the next node in the sequence.

2. How do you create a LinkedList in Java?
LinkedList<String> list = new LinkedList<>();

3. What are the main differences between ArrayList and LinkedList?
ArrayList uses a dynamic array internally and provides fast random access. LinkedList uses a doubly linked list and provides fast insertions and deletions.

4. How do you add elements to a LinkedList?
Using add(), addFirst(), and addLast() methods.

5. How do you remove elements from a LinkedList?
Using remove(), removeFirst(), and removeLast() methods.

6. How do you iterate over a LinkedList?
Using for-each loop, iterator, or for loop.

7. What is the time complexity of common LinkedList operations?
  • Access: O(n)
  • Add at beginning/end: O(1)
  • Insert at specific position: O(n)
  • Remove: O(n)
  • Search: O(n)

8. What is a doubly linked list?
A doubly linked list is a type of linked list where each node has a reference to both the next and the previous node.

9. What are the advantages and disadvantages of LinkedList?
Advantages: Dynamic size, efficient insertions and deletions.
Disadvantages: Higher memory usage due to storage of references, slower access time compared to arrays.

  • LinkedList is a doubly linked list implementing both List and Deque.
  • Good at adding and removing at the ends: addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, poll.

LinkedList holds first and last references to Node objects (item, next, prev). Adding at the ends is O(1) pointer updates; get(i) walks from the nearer end (so up to n/2 steps). Each node costs object header plus three references (about 24-32 bytes) on top of the element.

As a Deque it provides offerFirst, pollLast, peekFirst, descendingIterator. As a List it provides index methods. It allows nulls (ArrayDeque does not). It implements Queue so it can be a FIFO or work queue in single-threaded code.

  • Insert or remove is O(1) only when you already have the position (an iterator); finding the position is O(n).
  • It can act as a queue (offer/poll) or stack (push/pop).

  • Poor CPU cache locality makes iteration slower than ArrayList despite the same O(n).

Vector

Vector is a part of the Java Collection Framework and provides a dynamic array implementation, similar to ArrayList. The key difference is that Vector is synchronized (thread-safe). It is present in the java.util package.

Key Features of Vector


  • Underlying Data Structure - Growable array (resizable array).
  • Duplicates Allowed - Same element can appear multiple times.
  • Insertion Order Preserved - Elements maintain their insertion order.
  • Null Insertion Possible - Null values can be added.
  • Heterogeneous Objects Allowed - Can store different types (without generics).
  • Synchronized (Thread-Safe) - Every method in Vector is synchronized, making it safe for multi-threaded access.
  • Implements Serializable, Cloneable, and RandomAccess interfaces.
  • Best Choice for Retrieval - Due to index-based access (O(1)).
  • Legacy Class - Vector was present since JDK 1.0, before the Collection Framework was introduced in JDK 1.2.

Vector's 4 Constructors and Growth Policy


ConstructorWhat It DoesNew Capacity When Full

Vector(int initialCapacity)Empty vector with given capacity2 × current capacity
Vector(int initialCapacity, int incrementalCapacity)Empty vector, custom growth stepcurrent capacity + incrementalCapacity
Vector(Collection c)Vector pre-filled from an existing collection-

This is the key difference from ArrayList's growth policy: ArrayList grows by 50% of its current size, while Vector doubles its size by default (or grows by a fixed increment if one is specified in the constructor).

Vector Methods and Constructors


Methods


For Adding Objects:
  • add(Object o) - Adds element to the end.
  • add(int index, Object o) - Inserts element at specified index.
  • addElement(Object o) - Adds element to the end of the vector.

For Removing Objects:
  • remove(Object o) - Removes first occurrence of the element.
  • remove(int index) - Removes element at specified index.
  • removeElement(Object o) - Removes first occurrence of the element.

For Accessing Elements:
  • Object get(int index) - Returns element at the specified index.
  • Object ElementAt(int index) - Returns element at the specified index.
  • Object firstElement() - Returns the first element.
  • Object lastElement() - Returns the last element.

Other Methods:
  • int size() - Returns the number of elements in the Vector.
  • int capacity() - Returns the current capacity of the Vector.

2. Vector v = new Vector(int initialcapacity); - Create empty vector with specified initial capacity.
3. Vector v = new Vector(int initialcapacity, int incrementalcapacity); - Create vector with specified initial capacity and incremental capacity.
4. Vector v = new Vector(Collection c); - Create equivalent vector for given collection.

Before Iterator existed (JDK 1.0), Vector used Enumeration to traverse elements. It still works today via the elements() method, though Iterator is preferred in modern code.

Key Differences


1. Every method in ArrayList is non-synchronized; Every method in Vector is synchronized.
2. Multiple threads allowed on ArrayList (not thread safe); Only one thread allowed on Vector (thread safe).
3. ArrayList is faster (non-synchronized); Vector is slowest (synchronized/Thread Safe).
4. Threads not required to wait for ArrayList (performance high); Threads required to wait for Vector (performance low).
5. ArrayList introduced in 1.2 version (non-legacy); Vector introduced in 1.0 version (legacy class).

LegacyJava 1.2Java 1.0

Note: Legacy class means which comes from old generation. Ex: Stack & Vector are legacy classes.

Internal Working of Vector

Vector is the simplest internal structure of any collection covered in this course - there's no hashing, no tree, and no Node objects at all. It's just a plain Object[] array with synchronized methods wrapped around it.

Key Points


  • Vector internally holds: protected Object[] elementData; and protected int elementCount; (the array's allocated size vs how many slots are actually filled - this is exactly what capacity() vs size() report).
  • add(e) internally does: check if elementCount == elementData.length (array full?) → if so, grow the array first → then elementData[elementCount++] = e;.
  • get(index) internally does: return (E) elementData[index]; - a direct array read, which is why it's O(1) exactly like ArrayList.
  • Growth - if no capacityIncrement was given in the constructor, the new capacity is 2 * elementData.length (doubling); if a capacityIncrement WAS given, it's elementData.length + capacityIncrement instead.
  • Every one of these operations is wrapped in a synchronized block at the method level - the array logic itself is identical to ArrayList's.

AbstractList<E>  implements List<E>
△ extends
Vector<E>  implements List<E>, RandomAccess, Cloneable, Serializable
- elementData: Object[]

- capacityIncrement: int
△ extends
Stack<E>  adds 5 methods only: push, pop, peek, empty, search

The key contrast with HashSet/TreeSet: those two composed a completely separate object (a HashMap or TreeMap field). Stack does neither - it's pure inheritance, no composition at all. There is no second array anywhere; Stack's push()/pop()/peek() are thin one-line methods that call straight through to the SAME elementData array field it inherited from Vector:

public E push(E item) { addElement(item); return item; }
public E pop() { E obj = peek(); removeElementAt(size() - 1); return obj; }
public E peek() { return elementAt(size() - 1); }
This is exactly why Stack.get(0) works even though it "shouldn't" for a proper stack (mentioned in the Stack topic's "Stack vs ArrayDeque" comparison) - get(index) is just inherited straight from Vector/AbstractList with zero override, because Stack never restricted access to the underlying array in the first place.

  • Vector is a legacy resizable array whose methods are synchronized.
  • It works like ArrayList but doubles its capacity by default when full.
  • Extra legacy methods: addElement, elementAt, removeElement.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Thread-safe options: Collections.synchronizedList (same locking idea), CopyOnWriteArrayList (copy on every write, snapshot iteration), and ConcurrentLinkedQueue. Choose based on read to write ratio.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Synchronization on every method makes it slower than ArrayList when threads are not shared.
  • Individual methods are safe, but compound actions (check then add) still need external locking.
  • Prefer ArrayList, or Collections.synchronizedList or CopyOnWriteArrayList for concurrency.

Senior Notes

  • Vector exists for backward compatibility; new code should not use it.
  • Its Enumeration is not fail-fast, but its iterator is.
  • Its subclass Stack is also legacy; use ArrayDeque.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: assuming Vector makes compound operations atomic, iterating without holding the lock while other threads modify, and using it out of habit in new code. Synchronize on the vector for iteration or use a snapshot.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Uncontended synchronization is cheap on modern JVMs, but contended locks hurt scalability. Benchmarks usually show ArrayList several times faster in single-threaded code. Use fine-grained or lock-free structures for concurrency.

Real-world: legacy code (older Swing models, JDBC or JNDI APIs) still returns Vector or Enumeration. Convert at the boundary to modern types.

Stack

Stack is a subclass of Vector that implements the LIFO (Last In First Out) principle. The element that is pushed last onto the stack is the first one to be popped off. Stack is present in the java.util package.

Key Features


  • LIFO Order - Last element added is the first to be removed.
  • Extends Vector - Inherits all methods from Vector class.
  • Synchronized - Since it extends Vector, Stack is also thread-safe.

Stack-Specific Methods


  • push(Object obj) - Pushes an element onto the top of the stack.
  • pop() - Removes and returns the top element of the stack.
  • peek() - Returns the top element without removing it.
  • search(Object obj) - Returns the 1-based offset from top of the stack, or -1 if not found.

Constructor

  • Stack s = new Stack(); - Creates an empty Stack.

How Many Methods Does Stack Actually Have?

Stack itself declares only 5 methods - push(), pop(), peek(), empty(), search(). But because it extends Vector, every object of type Stack also carries all ~48 of Vector's methods (add, get, remove, contains, indexOf, subList, forEach, stream via Collection, etc.) - so in practice a Stack instance exposes ~53 usable public methods in total. See the Vector topic for the full method-by-method breakdown of everything Stack inherits.

Since Stack inherits from Vector, it also inherits Vector's legacy empty() method - functionally identical to isEmpty(), just named differently for stack terminology.

Stack Methods in Detail


Stack provides the following key methods:

1. Object push(Object obj); - For inserting an object to stack.
2. Object pop(); - To remove and return top of stack.
3. Object peek(); - To return the top of stack without removal of object.
4. int search(Object obj); - If specified object is available, returns its offset from top of stack. If not available, returns -1.

In the below example, elements A, B, C, D are pushed onto the stack. The search() method returns the LIFO-based offset from the top (D=1, C=2, B=3, A=4). Searching for an element not present ("Z") returns -1. The pop() method removes and returns the top element (D).

Typical algorithms: expression parsing (shunting yard), DFS without recursion, undo and redo, monotonic stack (next greater element), and matching delimiters. The call stack stores frames; recursion depth is limited by thread stack size.

Set Interface and HashSet

Set is a child interface of Collection, found in the java.util package. It represents a collection that does not allow duplicate elements. The Set interface is implemented by HashSet, LinkedHashSet, and TreeSet.

HashSet stores elements using a hash table internally. It is the most commonly used Set implementation.

Key Features of HashSet


  • No Duplicates Allowed - If you try to add a duplicate, the add() method returns false and the element is not added.
  • Insertion Order Not Preserved - Elements are stored based on their hash code, not insertion order.
  • Only One Null Allowed - You can add one null element, but not more than one (since duplicates are not allowed).
  • Non-Synchronized - Not thread-safe by default.
  • Heterogeneous Objects Allowed - Can store different types without generics.
  • Backed by HashMap - Internally, HashSet uses a HashMap to store elements.

HashSet Constructors


Constructors


1. HashSet h = new HashSet(); - Default initial capacity 16, load factor/fill ratio 0.75.
2. HashSet h = new HashSet(int initialCapacity); - Creates HashSet with given capacity.
3. HashSet h = new HashSet(int initialCapacity, float loadFactor); - Creates HashSet with given capacity and load factor.
4. HashSet h = new HashSet(Collection c); - Creates equivalent HashSet for given collection.

Load Factor / Fill Ratio


After filling 75% ratio, a new HashSet object is created. Load factor = 0.75 means after filling 75% of current capacity, a new larger HashSet is created.

HashSet: addAll() and forEach()


  • addAll(Collection) - Merges all elements of another collection into this HashSet (duplicates across the two are automatically dropped).
  • forEach(Consumer) - JDK 8 functional-style iteration using a lambda, instead of an explicit loop.

Deep Dive: HashSet's 4 Constructors and Mathematical Set Operations

Two things worth knowing beyond the individual method list: exactly how each constructor sizes the backing HashMap, and how HashSet's methods map directly onto the mathematical set operations (union, intersection, difference) from set theory.

Internal Working of HashSet

When you pass a duplicate element, the add() method returns false. Internally HashSet uses HashMap.

HashSet Implementation of add() Method


When you open HashSet implementation:

public class HashSet<E> extends AbstractSet<E> implements Set<E>, Cloneable, java.io.Serializable {
    private transient HashMap<E, Object> map;
    private static final Object PRESENT = new Object();

    public HashSet() {
        map = new HashMap<>();
    }

    public boolean add(E e) {
        return map.put(e, PRESENT) == null;
    }
}

How Uniqueness is Achieved


  • We achieve uniqueness through HashMap internally.
  • Each element is passed as key in HashMap with a dummy value PRESENT.
  • map.put(key, value) returns null if key is unique (added), returns old value if duplicate.
  • So if map.put(e, PRESENT) == null returns true → element added; returns false → duplicate.

Fresher Notes

  • HashSet stores unique elements with no guaranteed order and allows one null.
  • Backed by a HashMap; add returns false if the element already exists.
  • Operations (add, remove, contains) are O(1) on average.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

HashSet wraps a HashMap, storing each element as a key with a shared dummy value. The bucket index is (n - 1) & hash where hash spreads the high bits (h ^ (h >>> 16)). Collisions use a linked list, converted to a red-black tree when a bucket exceeds 8 entries and the table is at least 64. The table doubles at size greater than capacity times 0.75.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

A correct key class overrides hashCode and equals together (equal objects must have equal hash codes). Use immutable fields, Objects.hash or records. Set views: Set.copyOf for immutable, Collections.newSetFromMap for concurrent sets, ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() for a thread-safe set.

  • Uniqueness uses hashCode() then equals(): override both consistently in your classes.
  • Do not mutate fields used in hashCode while an object is in the set; it can get lost.
  • Set operations: addAll (union), retainAll (intersection), removeAll (difference).

Senior Notes

  • Iteration order can change as the set resizes; use LinkedHashSet for insertion order or TreeSet for sorted order.
  • Poor hashCode implementations degrade to O(n) (bucket collisions; Java 8 uses trees for large buckets).
  • Initial capacity and load factor (0.75) tune resizing; pre-size for large sets.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: overriding equals without hashCode (duplicates appear), mutable keys, expecting order, using HashSet (arrays use identity), and heavy hashCode implementations. Wrap arrays in a List or record.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Pre-size for known counts: capacity = expected / 0.75 + 1 to avoid rehashes. Bad hash functions cause collisions, and tree bins only help when keys are Comparable. Use a profiler or JMH to confirm.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: deduplicating events by id so each is processed once, and checking membership quickly in access control lists.

LinkedHashSet

LinkedHashSet is a child class of HashSet that maintains the insertion order of elements. Internally, it uses a hash table + doubly linked list combination. This linked list defines the iteration ordering, which is the order in which elements were inserted.

Key Features of LinkedHashSet


  • Maintains Insertion Order - Unlike HashSet, the order of elements is predictable and matches insertion order.
  • No Duplicates Allowed - Just like HashSet, duplicate elements are rejected.
  • Allows One Null - Only one null element is permitted.
  • Non-Synchronized - Not thread-safe by default.
  • Child of HashSet - Inherits all methods from HashSet.
  • Slightly Slower than HashSet - Due to the overhead of maintaining the linked list for ordering.

How Many Methods Does LinkedHashSet Actually Have?

LinkedHashSet declares zero new public methods of its own - it only overrides internal hooks so the hash table's iteration order matches insertion order. Every method you call on it (add, remove, contains, size, iterator, stream, removeIf, ...) is the exact same ~20 methods inherited from HashSet. TreeSet

TreeSet stores elements in sorted (ascending) order by default. Internally, it uses a Red-Black tree data structure, which is a self-balancing binary search tree.

Key Features of TreeSet


  • Sorted Order - Elements are automatically sorted in ascending/natural order.
  • No Duplicates - Duplicate elements are not allowed.
  • No Null - TreeSet does not allow null elements. Adding null throws NullPointerException (since Java 7).
  • Elements Must Be Comparable - All elements must implement the Comparable interface, or a Comparator must be provided at construction time.
  • Non-Synchronized - Not thread-safe by default.
  • Implements NavigableSet - Provides navigation methods like floor(), ceiling(), lower(), higher().

Case-Sensitive Sorting: Numbers, Capitals, then Lowercase

Just like ArrayList sorting, TreeSet's natural ordering for Strings follows ASCII value - numbers first, then capital letters, then lowercase letters.

TreeSet Details

TreeSet stores elements in sorted ascending order. Uses balanced tree (Red-Black tree) internally.

Important Rules


  • Heterogeneous objects NOT allowed - throws ClassCastException.
  • Null not allowed - throws NullPointerException (since Java 7).
  • All elements must implement Comparable interface or provide Comparator.

SortedSet - Parent Interface of TreeSet


SortedSet is the child interface of Set that TreeSet implements. Use it when you want to represent a group of objects according to some sorting order, with duplicates not allowed. It defines 2 key methods:

  • Object first() - Returns the first (smallest) element of the sorted set.
  • Object last() - Returns the last (largest) element of the sorted set.

Constructors


1. TreeSet t = new TreeSet(); - Creates empty TreeSet with natural sorting order.
2. TreeSet t = new TreeSet(Comparator c); - Creates empty TreeSet with customized sorting.
3. TreeSet t = new TreeSet(Collection c); - Creates TreeSet for given collection.
4. TreeSet t = new TreeSet(SortedSet s); - Creates TreeSet for given SortedSet.

TreeSet Navigation Methods

TreeSet implements the NavigableSet interface, which provides several useful navigation methods:

  • ceiling(e) - Smallest element that is >= the given element.
  • floor(e) - Largest element that is <= the given element.
  • higher(e) - Smallest element strictly > the given element (null if none).
  • lower(e) - Largest element strictly < the given element (null if none).
  • pollFirst() - Removes and returns the smallest element (null if empty).
  • pollLast() - Removes and returns the largest element (null if empty).
  • headSet(e) - Returns elements strictly less than the given element.
  • isEmpty() / remove(e) / clear() - Standard checks and mutations.

Internal Working of TreeSet

Just like HashSet delegates to a HashMap, TreeSet delegates to a TreeMap - same composition pattern, different backing structure. Elements you add become keys in the hidden map, again paired with the same dummy PRESENT value, but this time the map keeps them in a Red-Black tree instead of hash buckets - which is exactly why TreeSet iterates in sorted order for free.

Key Points


  • TreeSet internally creates: private transient NavigableMap<E, Object> m; (typed as the interface, but a TreeMap instance underneath).
  • add(e) internally calls: m.put(e, PRESENT) - same trick as HashSet's add().
  • first() / last() internally call: m.firstKey() / m.lastKey().
  • ceiling(e) / floor(e) / higher(e) / lower(e) internally call the identically-named key methods on the map (ceilingKey(), floorKey(), etc.) - see the TreeMap topic's "Internal Working" for how those actually walk the Red-Black tree.
  • headSet()/tailSet()/subSet() internally call headMap()/tailMap()/subMap() and wrap the resulting key view back into a Set.

The same is-a vs has-a split as HashSet, but one level up the interface hierarchy - TreeSet implements the richer NavigableSet interface, and composes a NavigableMap (concretely a TreeMap) instead of a plain HashMap.

NavigableSet itself sits in a parallel hierarchy to NavigableMap: Set ← SortedSet ← NavigableSet, mirroring Map ← SortedMap ← NavigableMap almost method-for-method (first/last, ceiling/floor/higher/lower, headSet/tailSet/subSet mirroring headMap/tailMap/subMap). That symmetry is not an accident - it's why every navigation method on TreeSet has a one-line delegation to the identically-shaped method on its internal map.

Interview Questions on Set


1. What is a Set in Java?
A Set is a collection that does not allow duplicate elements. It models the mathematical set abstraction and is part of the Java Collections Framework.

2. What are the main implementations of the Set interface?
  • HashSet - Uses a hash table, constant-time performance for basic operations.
  • LinkedHashSet - Maintains a linked list of entries in insertion order.
  • TreeSet - Implements NavigableSet, uses a Red-Black tree, orders elements by value.

3. How do you create a HashSet in Java?
Set<String> set = new HashSet<>();

4. What is the difference between HashSet and TreeSet?
HashSet does not maintain any order of its elements, while TreeSet maintains elements in sorted order. HashSet provides constant-time performance for basic operations, whereas TreeSet provides log-time performance.

5. How do you check if a Set contains a specific element?
Using the contains() method: boolean containsElement = set.contains("element");

6. How do you remove an element from a Set?
Using the remove() method: set.remove("element");

7. What is the time complexity of basic operations in a HashSet?
The time complexity for basic operations (add, remove, contains) in a HashSet is O(1) on average.

8. What is LinkedHashSet and when would you use it?
LinkedHashSet is an implementation of the Set interface that maintains a doubly-linked list across all elements, preserving insertion order. Use it when you need a set that maintains the order elements were added.

9. How do you iterate over a Set?
Using a for-each loop or an Iterator, same as any other Collection.

10. What is the difference between Set and List in Java?
Set does not allow duplicate elements and does not maintain any order (except LinkedHashSet and TreeSet), while List allows duplicate elements and maintains insertion order.

Map Interface and HashMap

The Map interface represents a collection of key-value pairs. Unlike List and Set, Map is not part of the Collection hierarchy - it is a separate interface. Each key maps to exactly one value.

Key Features of Map


  • Key-Value Pairs - Each entry consists of a key and its associated value.
  • No Duplicate Keys - Each key must be unique. If you put a value with an existing key, the old value is replaced.
  • Values May Be Duplicated - Multiple keys can map to the same value.
  • Both Keys and Values Are Objects - Primitives must be wrapped in their wrapper classes.

HashMap is the most commonly used Map implementation. It stores entries in a hash table and provides O(1) average time for get and put operations.

  • HashMap uses hashing mechanism. When key-value pair is added, hash code of key is computed.

Put Operation


Compute hash -> find bucket -> if empty, add node; if collision, traverse list and compare keys using equals(). If key found, update value; if not, add new node.

Get Operation


Compute hash -> find bucket -> traverse list comparing keys.

Treeification


When bucket size >= 8, linked list converts to balanced Red-Black tree for O(log n) lookup.

Resize


When entries > capacity * loadFactor, capacity doubles and all entries rehashed.

LinkedHashMap

LinkedHashMap extends HashMap and maintains the insertion order of its entries. Internally, it uses a hash table + doubly linked list. The linked list preserves the order in which entries were inserted.

Key Features of LinkedHashMap


  • Maintains Insertion Order - Entries are iterated in the order they were added.
  • Extends HashMap - Inherits all HashMap methods and behavior.
  • Allows One Null Key - Like HashMap, permits one null key and multiple null values.
  • Non-Synchronized - Not thread-safe by default.
  • Slightly Slower than HashMap - Due to the linked list maintenance overhead.

How Many Methods Does LinkedHashMap Actually Have?

LinkedHashMap declares zero new public methods - it only overrides internal hooks (like the protected removeEldestEntry(), useful for building an LRU cache) so entries iterate in insertion order instead of hash-bucket order. Every method you call (put, get, remove, computeIfAbsent, merge, entrySet, ...) is the exact same ~27 methods inherited from HashMap. See the HashMap topic for the full method-by-method breakdown.

Comparison


  • HashMap: No order guarantee, slightly faster, less memory

  • Both allow one null key, duplicate values
  • Both are non-synchronized

Deep Dive: LinkedHashMap's Real Distinguishing Feature

Since every public method is inherited unchanged from HashMap, LinkedHashMap's actual API surface worth knowing is its 5 constructors (HashMap only has 4 - the extra one is unique to LinkedHashMap) and one protected method you're meant to override.

When accessOrder is true, iteration order becomes "least recently accessed first" instead of insertion order - every get()/put() moves that entry to the end of the internal linked list. This one constructor is the entire foundation of building an LRU cache.

removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry eldest) - a protected method that always returns false by default (never auto-removes anything). Override it to return true once the map exceeds a size limit, and LinkedHashMap will automatically evict the eldest entry on every put() - combined with accessOrder=true, this turns a plain map into a working LRU (Least Recently Used) cache in about 10 lines of code.

  • LinkedHashMap is a HashMap that remembers insertion order (or access order).
  • Iteration follows the order the keys were added; re-putting an existing key does not change its position.

Internal Working of TreeMap

TreeMap has a completely different internal structure from HashMap - there's no hashing, no buckets, and no array at all. Every entry is a node in a Red-Black tree (a self-balancing binary search tree), and every operation is driven entirely by comparison (via Comparable or a supplied Comparator), not hash codes.

The Red-Black Tree Rules

A Red-Black tree stays balanced by enforcing 4 simple coloring rules on every insert/delete:

RuleWhat It Guarantees
Every node is RED or BLACKJust a 1-bit color flag stored per node
The root is always BLACKFixes a reference point for the other rules
Every RED node has two BLACK children (no two REDs in a row)Prevents any path from being disproportionately "red-heavy"
Every path from a node to its descendant null leaves has the same number of BLACK nodesThe actual balance guarantee - the longest possible path is never more than 2× the shortest, which is what keeps height at O(log n)

key, valueThe actual entry data
left, rightReferences to the left/right child nodes
parentReference back up the tree - needed to fix balance after insert/delete
colorRED or BLACK - the flag the rebalancing algorithm reads and flips

How put(key, value) Actually Works


1. Traverse from the root - at each node, call compareTo() (or the supplied Comparator.compare()) between the new key and the current node's key.
2. Go left if the new key is smaller, go right if larger, until an empty spot is found (or an equal key is found, in which case the value is just replaced).
3. Insert the new node as RED at that spot (inserting red first, rather than black, keeps the black-height rule intact immediately).
4. Fix-up pass - walk back up from the new node checking for violations (two reds in a row). Violations are resolved with a mix of recoloring and rotations (single or double, left or right) until all 4 rules hold again.

Why this matters: because every step is a comparison, TreeMap's performance depends entirely on how cheap and correct your compareTo()/Comparator is - unlike HashMap, there's no hashCode() involved anywhere in a TreeMap.

Rebalances viaResize (doubling capacity) + treeification of individual bucketsRotations + recoloring on every insert/delete
get/put time complexityO(1) average, O(log n) worst case (post-treeification)O(log n) always, guaranteed by the tree balance rules

TreeMap sits at the bottom of its own delegation chain too (nothing composes it the way HashSet composes HashMap) - but its internal node type is structurally different from HashMap's Node in a way worth diagramming explicitly.

key, value, left, right, parent, color

This is the structural reason TreeMap doesn't need (or have) an array field at all - HashMap's table array is what a hash structure fundamentally requires, while a tree only ever needs one entry point (root) plus the parent/child pointers threaded through the Entry nodes themselves.

Memory Diagram: What put() Actually Builds on the Heap

Same exercise as HashMap's diagram, but forming a tree with real key-value pairs instead of a bucket array - directly comparable to TreeSet's memory diagram, just with an actual value field instead of the shared PRESENT dummy.

HEAP - after treeMap.put(20,"Twenty"); put(10,"Ten"); put(30,"Thirty");

{key=20, value="Twenty", left → Entry@E2, right → Entry@E3, parent → null}
Entry@E2 (RED)
{key=10, value="Ten", left→null, right→null, parent→E1} 		Entry@E3 (RED)
{key=30, value="Thirty", left→null, right→null, parent→E1}

Tracing get(10): start at root E1 (key=20) → compareTo says 10 < 20, follow left to E2 (key=10) → keys match, return E2's value field ("Ten") directly. Three pointer hops total, matching the O(log n) guarantee - no array indexing, no hash computation, purely following left/right references down from root.

Why remove() is more involved than insert(): deleting E1 (the root) isn't as simple as clearing a reference - since E1 has two children, the tree must first find E1's in-order successor (the leftmost node of its right subtree) to replace it with, then re-run the same rotation/recolor fix-up logic on whatever node ends up where the deleted one was. This is why TreeMap deletion, while still O(log n), does meaningfully more pointer surgery per call than a HashMap bucket removal (which is just next reassignment).

Hashtable

Hashtable is a synchronized (thread-safe) implementation of the Map interface. It is a legacy class that was part of Java since JDK 1.0, before the Collection Framework was introduced.

Key Features of Hashtable


  • Synchronized (Thread-Safe) - Every method is synchronized, making it safe for multi-threaded access.
  • No Null Keys or Values - Hashtable does not allow null keys or null values. Attempting to use null throws NullPointerException.
  • Legacy Class - Present since JDK 1.0. Implements the legacy Dictionary class as well as Map interface.
  • Similar to HashMap - Functionally similar but synchronized and no null allowed.
  • Slower than HashMap - Due to synchronization overhead on every method call.
  • Different Default Capacity - Hashtable starts with an initial default capacity of 11 (and a load factor of 0.75), unlike HashMap's default capacity of 16.

HashMap vs Hashtable


Comparison


  • HashMap: Non-synchronized, allows one null key & multiple null values, introduced in 1.2, faster, Iterator is fail-fast
  • Hashtable: Synchronized (thread safe), NO null keys or values, introduced in 1.0 (legacy), slower, Enumerator is not fail-fast
  • Both: Store key-value pairs, no duplicate keys

Hashtable - Complete Method Reference (~29 Methods)

Hashtable's method set is almost identical to HashMap's, plus two legacy Enumeration-based methods left over from JDK 1.0 (predating even the Iterator interface). Grouped by purpose:

CategoryMethods
1. Shared with HashMapput, get, remove, containsKey, containsValue, size, isEmpty, clear, keySet, values, entrySet, putAll, putIfAbsent, getOrDefault, replace, replaceAll, compute*, merge, forEach - all identical to HashMap
2. Legacy (unique to Hashtable/Dictionary)keys() - Enumeration of keys, elements() - Enumeration of values, contains(Object) - legacy alias for containsValue()
3. Otherclone(), equals(Object), hashCode(), toString()

Since all the shared methods behave exactly like HashMap (just synchronized, and rejecting null), see the HashMap topic for their individual examples - only the legacy Enumeration methods are shown separately below.
Hashtable's Legacy Methods - Separate Example for Each

Internal Working of Hashtable

Hashtable looks like "synchronized HashMap" from the outside, but its internals actually predate HashMap by years (JDK 1.0 vs JDK 1.2) and differ in several concrete ways that rarely get mentioned.

1. Prime-Number Capacity + Modulo Indexing (Not Power-of-2 + Bitwise AND)


AspectHashMapHashtable
Default capacity16 (power of 2)11 (arbitrary, historically prime-friendly)
Bucket index formula(n - 1) & hash - bitwise AND, very fast(hash & 0x7FFFFFFF) % table.length - modulo, slower
Why the difference mattersBitwise AND only gives even bucket distribution when capacity is a power of 2Modulo works correctly for any capacity, at the cost of a slower operation per put/get
Growth formulanewCapacity = oldCapacity × 2 (clean doubling)newCapacity = (oldCapacity × 2) + 1 (double, then +1)

2. No Treeification - Ever

Unlike HashMap (which converts a heavily-collided bucket to a Red-Black tree once it has 8+ nodes AND the table has 64+ buckets), Hashtable's buckets stay linked lists forever, no matter how many entries collide. Worst-case lookup in a single bucket is always O(n) in Hashtable, while HashMap caps it at O(log n) since Java 8.

3. Class Hierarchy - Dictionary, Not Just Map

Hashtable is one of the few classes that implements both the legacy abstract class Dictionary<K,V> (JDK 1.0, now obsolete) and the modern Map<K,V> interface (added in 1.2 to retrofit it into the Collection Framework) - that dual inheritance is why it has both legacy methods (keys(), elements(), put() returning the old value like Dictionary specified) and modern Map methods (keySet(), entrySet(), computeIfAbsent(), etc.) side by side.

4. Coarse-Grained Locking

Every public method (put, get, remove, size, even isEmpty) is declared synchronized, meaning it acquires the intrinsic lock on the entire Hashtable object before doing anything. Two threads calling get() on different, unrelated keys still block each other - there is no concept of partial/segment locking the way ConcurrentHashMap has.

5. Null Rejection Happens Immediately, Not Via Bucket Logic

HashMap has special-cased handling that lets a null key live in bucket 0. Hashtable has no such path - put() explicitly checks if (value == null) throw new NullPointerException() right at the top, before any hashing happens at all (and a null key throws too, since key.hashCode() would NPE regardless).

Deep Dive: The JDK 8 Map Default Methods on Hashtable - and Where Null-Handling Differs

Hashtable inherits putIfAbsent, getOrDefault, computeIfAbsent, computeIfPresent, compute, merge, replaceAll, forEach from the Map interface's default methods, exactly like HashMap does. They work the same day-to-day - but Hashtable's blanket "no nulls, ever" rule still applies underneath, which trips people up on a couple of these specifically.

Deep Dive: Hashtable's 4 Constructors, putAll(), and Its Views

Rounding out the reference: all 4 constructors side by side (note the default capacity is 11, not 16 - see Internal Working above for why), plus putAll(), keySet()/values() individually, and clone()/equals()/hashCode()/toString() shown directly on Hashtable.

Class Diagram: Hashtable's Unusual Dual Inheritance

Every other Map implementation in this course (HashMap, TreeMap, LinkedHashMap) reaches Map<K,V> through a single path: AbstractMap implements Map. Hashtable is the odd one out - it's the only class here that both extends an abstract class and implements an interface to get there, a leftover from being designed 2 years before the Collection Framework existed.

Dictionary<K,V>
(abstract class, JDK 1.0, obsolete) 		«interface» Map<K,V>
(JDK 1.2, retrofitted)
△ extends △ implements
Hashtable<K,V>  implements Map<K,V>, Cloneable, Serializable
- table: Entry<K,V>[]

Hashtable's node type - a bucket-list node, same shape as HashMap's, different class entirely

hash, key, value, next
always a linked list - Hashtable has no TreeNode equivalent, ever

Why this matters beyond trivia: because Hashtable inherits from Dictionary, its put() method's return-value contract and its size()/isEmpty() behavior were fixed by the 1996-era Dictionary spec first, then Map's newer interface was bolted on afterward to make it collection-framework-compatible. That's the direct cause of the legacy/modern method duplication seen in the method reference table earlier (keys() alongside keySet(), elements() alongside values()) - two API generations coexisting in one class, unlike any other Map implementation covered here.

Memory Diagram: Bucket Placement AND the Synchronization Lock

Two things worth diagramming for Hashtable that don't apply to HashMap at all: the modulo-based bucket index (different arithmetic, possibly a different bucket than HashMap would choose for the same key), and the intrinsic lock every method acquires.

HEAP - after ht.put("Pankaj", 90000) on a fresh Hashtable (default capacity 11)
Hashtable@H
table[11] → bucket array 		→ index = (hash & 0x7FFFFFFF) % 11
table[index] → Entry@N1
{hash, key→"Pankaj", value→90000, next→null}

Contrast with HashMap's diagram: HashMap computed its bucket with (n-1) & hash against a capacity-16 table; Hashtable computes it with % 11 against a capacity-11 table. Same key, same hashCode() value going in, but a different index arithmetic means the two structures don't even necessarily agree on which bucket "Pankaj" belongs in - there's no equivalence between a HashMap bucket number and a Hashtable bucket number for the same key.

The Lock: What synchronized Actually Guards


Hashtable@H's object header
monitor (intrinsic lock) - currently held by Thread-1
Thread-1: inside ht.put("A", 1)
holds the lock, executing normally 		Thread-2: calls ht.get("Z")
BLOCKED waiting for the same lock - even though "A" and "Z" are unrelated keys in different buckets

The key point this diagram makes visible: the lock lives on the Hashtable object itself, not on individual buckets - so Thread-2's get("Z") has to wait even though it will never touch the same Entry that Thread-1 is modifying. This single whole-object lock is exactly what a real ConcurrentHashMap replaces with much finer-grained locking (historically per-segment, now per-bin in modern JDKs), letting Thread-1 and Thread-2 proceed at the same time as long as they land in different buckets.

When to use Hashtable vs ConcurrentHashMap


  • Hashtable synchronizes every method (entire table locked) - poor performance
  • ConcurrentHashMap uses per-bin locking (CAS on empty bins plus synchronized on the bin head; the Java 7 Segment array was removed in Java 8) - much better concurrent performance
  • ConcurrentHashMap allows concurrent reads without locking
  • ConcurrentHashMap is preferred for multi-threaded applications since Java 5
  • Hashtable is legacy, ConcurrentHashMap is modern replacement

Fresher Notes

  • Hashtable is a legacy, synchronized key-value collection; it does not allow null keys or values.
  • It predates the Collections Framework and was retrofitted to implement Map.
  • Methods are synchronized, so it is slower than HashMap in single-threaded use.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Hashtable uses an array of Entry chains, indexes with (hash & 0x7FFFFFFF) % table.length (modulo, not a mask), grows to 2 * n + 1, and every public method is synchronized on the table. It never treeifies chains. Its Enumerator is not fail-fast while the iterator is.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Modern choices: ConcurrentHashMap (atomic compute, merge, bulk operations), Collections.synchronizedMap (explicit lock for iteration), immutable Map.of for constants. Properties still matters for config files and system properties.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Differences from HashMap: synchronized, no nulls, uses Enumeration, and its iteration order is not predictable.
  • Use ConcurrentHashMap for thread-safe maps instead.
  • Properties extends Hashtable and loads key-value files.

Senior Notes

  • Locking the whole table limits concurrency; ConcurrentHashMap locks per bin and uses CAS.
  • Compound actions (check then put) are still not atomic on Hashtable.
  • You mostly meet it in legacy code and via Properties.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: expecting nulls to work, thinking compound operations are atomic, holding the table lock for long work, and iterating without locking the table. Prefer atomic methods.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

One lock for the whole table serializes every operation, limiting throughput as threads grow. ConcurrentHashMap reads without locking and locks per bin on writes, so it scales much better.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: legacy JNDI environments and JDBC connection properties still use Hashtable and Properties; convert to Map at the edge.

Comparable Interface

The Comparable interface is found in the java.lang package. It is used to define the natural ordering of objects. A class that implements Comparable can have its objects sorted automatically using Collections.sort(List) or Arrays.sort().

Key Points


  • Package: java.lang (imported automatically).
  • Method: Contains a single method - compareTo(Object o).
  • Return Value:
  - Returns negative integer if the current object is less than the other object.
  - Returns zero if the current object is equal to the other object.
  - Returns positive integer if the current object is greater than the other object.
  • Usage: Used with Collections.sort(List) for natural ordering.
  • Modifies the Original Class: The class itself must implement Comparable and define compareTo().

Comparable - Complete Method Reference

The Comparable interface itself declares only 1 method - that's the whole contract. But writing a correct compareTo() body almost always means reaching for one of the JDK's built-in static compare() helpers below, instead of risky manual subtraction (see the "Internal Working" section for why subtraction is a real bug source).

MethodDescriptionReturn Type
compareTo(T o)The single method Comparable declares - compares this object with the specified object for orderint
Integer.compare(int, int)Safe comparison of two int values - use this instead of a - b inside compareTo()int
Double.compare(double, double)Safe comparison of two double values, correctly handles NaN and -0.0/+0.0int
Long.compare(long, long)Safe comparison of two long valuesint
Boolean.compare(boolean, boolean)Compares two booleans - false is considered less than trueint
String.compareTo(String)Lexicographic (dictionary-order) comparison - String itself implements Comparable<String>int
String.compareToIgnoreCase(String)Same as compareTo() but case-insensitiveint
Objects.compare(T, T, Comparator)Null-safe comparison of two objects using a supplied Comparatorint

Deep Dive: Multi-Field compareTo() and Enum's Built-in Ordering

Comparable itself has no chaining helpers like Comparator's thenComparing() - so multi-field natural ordering has to either be written by hand, field by field, or delegate to a Comparator chain internally. Both approaches are shown below, plus a look at how enum gets Comparable for free.

Deep Dive Part 2: Primitive Arrays Don't Use Comparable At All

A commonly-missed interview nuance: Arrays.sort() behaves completely differently depending on whether you give it a primitive array or an object array - and only one of the two paths ever touches Comparable.

CallAlgorithm UsedUses Comparable?
Arrays.sort(int[] a) (and other primitive array types)Dual-Pivot QuicksortNo - primitives have no compareTo() to call; values are compared directly with </>
Arrays.sort(Object[] a)TimSortYes - calls each element's compareTo()

This is also why the "Comparison method violates its general contract!" exception from earlier can only happen when sorting an object array (or a List) - a primitive int[] array physically cannot trigger it, since there's no compareTo() involved to violate any contract.

Implementing Comparable with Employee Class

The Comparable interface allows us to define the natural ordering for custom objects. Here we implement Comparable with an Employee class to sort data by salary.

How compareTo() Works


• If salary == employee.salary → return 0 (equal).
• If salary > employee.salary → return 1 (greater).
• If salary < employee.salary → return -1 (lesser).

After calling Collections.sort(al), the list is sorted in ascending order by salary. The second example demonstrates sorting Student objects by age using the same approach.

Benefits of Comparable


Key Benefits


  • 1. Natural Ordering: Defines a consistent way to compare objects. Once implemented, objects can be sorted anywhere without specifying how to sort them.

  • 2. Simplifies Code: Eliminates the need for custom comparator classes for simple comparisons. Just call Collections.sort(list) without passing any extra argument.

  • 3. Integration with Collections: Works seamlessly with Java's collection framework for sorting lists, sets, and maps. TreeSet and TreeMap automatically use Comparable to maintain sorted order.

Internal Working of Comparable

compareTo() isn't just a method you implement and forget - it's called internally, repeatedly, by several different pieces of JDK machinery, and each one has its own expectations.

CallerHow It Uses compareTo() Internally
Collections.sort(list) / Arrays.sort(objArray)Runs TimSort (a hybrid merge/insertion sort, since Java 7) - repeatedly calls a.compareTo(b) to decide merge order and to detect already-sorted runs to skip.
TreeSet / TreeMapOn every add()/put(), walks the Red-Black tree from the root, calling compareTo() at each node to decide whether to go left (negative) or right (positive), until it finds the correct insertion point.
PriorityQueueCalls compareTo() while sifting a new element up/down the binary heap to keep the smallest element at the root.
Collections.max() / min()Linear scan, calling compareTo() against the current best candidate on each element.

The Contract TimSort Actually Enforces at Runtime

Since Java 7, Arrays.sort() / Collections.sort() on objects don't just trust your compareTo() - TimSort actively detects contract violations (non-transitive or inconsistent comparisons) on large enough inputs and throws:
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract!
This is one of the most common real-world Comparable/Comparator bugs in production Java code - usually caused by a compareTo() that isn't perfectly transitive (e.g., mixing multiple fields with subtraction that can overflow, or comparing floating-point values inconsistently).

Memory Diagram: Where compareTo() Actually Lives

The key insight a diagram makes obvious: with Comparable, the comparison logic is baked into the object's own class in the Metaspace - there is no separate "comparator object" anywhere in memory. Sorting just means asking each object to compare itself to another.

HEAP
List<Person> people
ref[0] → Person@A
ref[1] → Person@B 		→ Person@A {name="Baji", age=28}
class pointer ↓

Person@B {name="Ann", age=25}
class pointer ↓
METASPACE (shared by ALL Person instances)
Person.class
bytecode for: int compareTo(Person other) { return Integer.compare(this.age, other.age); }

What happens when personA.compareTo(personB) runs: the JVM reads personA's class pointer (a hidden field in every object's header) to find Person.class in Metaspace, locates the compareTo() bytecode there (only ONE copy exists, shared by every Person object), and executes it with this = personA and the argument other = personB. No extra object was created just to do the comparison - the logic was already sitting in the class metadata.

Class Diagram: Comparable and Its Ecosystem

A UML view of the same idea from a different angle - not memory layout this time, but the type relationships. Notice every implementing class points UP to the single interface (realization), while every JDK consumer points DOWN to it as a dependency - Comparable sits at the center of a hub, not a chain.

«interface»

△ realizes (implements)

depends on (calls .compareTo() internally) ⇩
Collections.sort() / Arrays.sort() TreeSet / TreeMap PriorityQueue Collections.max()/min()

Reading this diagram: any class in the top row can be dropped straight into any consumer in the bottom row with zero extra code - that's the entire value proposition of Comparable. The trade-off the diagram doesn't show: because the interface is realized by the class itself, a class can only ever have one compareTo() implementation active at a time - which is exactly the gap Comparator (next topic) exists to fill.

Fresher Notes

  • Comparable<T> defines the natural order of a class through int compareTo(T other).
  • Return negative, zero or positive when this is less than, equal to or greater than other.
  • Sorting methods like Collections.sort and TreeSet use it.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Collections.sort and Arrays.sort for objects use TimSort (merge sort plus insertion sort), which is stable and calls compareTo. Sorted structures (TreeMap, TreeSet, PriorityQueue) call compareTo on every insert. Contract: sgn(x.compareTo(y)) == -sgn(y.compareTo(x)), transitive, and x.compareTo(y)==0 implies the same sign against any z.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Implement with Comparator helpers inside compareTo for multi-field order, and keep it consistent with equals and hashCode. For records, declare Comparable explicitly. Enums compare by declaration order. Comparable.compareTo(null) should throw NullPointerException.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Keep compareTo consistent with equals where possible; use Integer.compare instead of subtraction (overflow).
  • A class has only one natural order; use Comparator for others.
  • String, Integer, LocalDate and many core classes implement Comparable.

Senior Notes

  • The contract: sign symmetry, transitivity and consistency; violating it causes "Comparison method violates its general contract" errors in TimSort.
  • Inconsistent with equals leads to surprising behavior in TreeSet and TreeMap.
  • Records and enums: enums are Comparable by ordinal; records need an explicit implementation.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: comparing doubles with subtraction, forgetting a tiebreaker (equal elements vanish in sets), comparing only part of the state, and non-transitive logic (rock-paper-scissors). Use Double.compare for floating point.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

compareTo is called O(n log n) times in a sort, so keep it cheap: compare primitive fields first, cache expensive derived keys (Schwartzian transform), and avoid allocations inside compareTo.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: semantic version ordering, money amounts, and priority tasks in a PriorityQueue.
