Comparator Interface

The Comparator interface is found in the java.util package. It is used for customized sorting - defining sorting logic externally, without modifying the original class.

Key Points


  • Package: java.util (must be imported).
  • Methods: Contains compare(Object o1, Object o2) and equals(Object obj) methods.
  • Return Value of compare():
  - Returns negative integer if o1 is less than o2.
  - Returns zero if o1 is equal to o2.
  - Returns positive integer if o1 is greater than o2.
  • Does Not Modify Original Class: Sorting logic is defined in a separate class or lambda expression.
  • Multiple Sort Orders: You can create multiple Comparators for different sorting criteria.
  • Usage: Used with Collections.sort(List, Comparator) or as constructor argument for TreeSet/TreeMap.

Comparator with Multiple Sorting Criteria

We can use Comparator to define our own sorting (customized sorting order). Unlike Comparable, Comparator does not require modifying the original class.

Key Points


  • Comparator defines 2 methods: public int compare(Object obj1, Object obj2) and public boolean equals().
  • Implementing equals() is optional since it is already available from the Object class.
  • We can create multiple Comparator classes (e.g., NameComparator, SalaryComparator) to sort by different fields.

The example below shows a Student class with separate NameComparator and SalaryComparator classes to sort by name and salary respectively.

Comparator - Complete Method Reference (~15 Methods)

Classic code writes a whole separate class (like NameComparator above) just to implement compare(). JDK 8 added default/static methods directly on the Comparator interface that make this dramatically shorter - these are the methods senior Java code actually uses today. Grouped by purpose:

1. Core (abstract)compare(T, T)
2. Static FactoriesnaturalOrder(), reverseOrder(), comparing(Function), comparing(Function, Comparator), comparingInt/Long/Double(ToXFunction)
3. Chaining (default methods)reversed(), thenComparing(Comparator), thenComparing(Function), thenComparing(Function, Comparator), thenComparingInt/Long/Double(ToXFunction)
4. Null HandlingnullsFirst(Comparator), nullsLast(Comparator)

The table above lists 15 methods; the earlier examples covered the ones used 90% of the time. These are the remaining overloads - less common, but each solves a specific real problem.

Deep Dive Part 2: The Last Overload, and the 4 Ways to Write a Comparator

Closing out the method reference with thenComparingInt() (the one overload not yet shown), then a side-by-side of every syntax Java offers for implementing the exact same Comparator - useful to recognize all four in the wild, even if you'd only ever write the last one today.

Comparable vs Comparator - Comparison Table


Key Differences


  • 1. Comparable provides single sorting sequence; Comparator provides multiple sorting sequences.

  • 2. Comparable affects the original class (actual class is modified); Comparator does not affect the original class.

  • 3. Comparable provides compareTo() method; Comparator provides compare() method.

  • 4. Comparable is in java.lang package; Comparator is in java.util package.

  • 5. For Comparable: Collections.sort(List); For Comparator: Collections.sort(List, Comparator).

  • 6. Comparable is for default natural sorting order; Comparator is for customized sorting order.

  • 7. Comparable defines only 1 method (compareTo); Comparator defines 2 methods (compare and equals).

Internal Working of Comparator

Like Comparable, a plain compare() call is only half the story - the interesting internals are in how JDK collections invoke it and how the JDK 8 chaining methods are actually implemented.

CallerHow It Uses compare() Internally
Collections.sort(list, cmp) / list.sort(cmp)Same TimSort algorithm as Comparable-based sorting, except every comparison calls cmp.compare(a, b) instead of a.compareTo(b) - the algorithm itself doesn't change, only where the comparison decision comes from.
new TreeSet<>(comparator) / new TreeMap<>(comparator)When a Comparator is supplied to the constructor, the tree stores it internally and uses comparator.compare(a, b) for every Red-Black tree traversal - it completely ignores the elements' own compareTo(), even if they implement Comparable.
PriorityQueue(comparator)Same idea - the supplied Comparator drives every sift-up/sift-down comparison in the binary heap instead of natural ordering.

How thenComparing() and reversed() Are Actually Implemented

These aren't magic - they're just lambdas that wrap the original compare() call. Conceptually (simplified from the real JDK source):

reversed()return (a, b) -> this.compare(b, a); - simply swaps the argument order
thenComparing(other)return (a, b) -> { int r = this.compare(a, b); return r != 0 ? r : other.compare(a, b); }; - only consults the next comparator if the first result was a tie (0)
naturalOrder()return (a, b) -> a.compareTo(b); - a static Comparator that just delegates back to Comparable

This is why chaining comparing(A).thenComparing(B).thenComparing(C) costs almost nothing extra at runtime for already-decided comparisons - each link in the chain is skipped entirely unless every earlier one returned exactly 0.

The contrast with Comparable's diagram is the whole point: with Comparator, the comparison logic lives in a completely separate object that has no relationship to the elements being compared. The elements stay "dumb" - all the intelligence sits in one independent Comparator instance.

Why chaining is cheap: comparing(A).thenComparing(B) doesn't merge any logic together - it creates a new wrapper Comparator object that holds a reference to the first one and calls it first, only reaching into the second (delegate) object if the first returned 0. This is why the diagram shows a chain of small objects, each just forwarding to the next - identical in spirit to a linked list, not a single fused method.

The mirror image of Comparable's diagram - and the difference is the entire point of the interface's existence. That one distinction is why you can have unlimited Comparators per class, but only one Comparable.

Internal Working of HashSet

HashSet is internally backed by a HashMap. When you create a HashSet, it creates a HashMap object behind the scenes. The elements you add to the HashSet are stored as keys in the underlying HashMap, and a constant dummy object called PRESENT is used as the value for every key.

Why No Duplicates?

Since HashMap does not allow duplicate keys, HashSet automatically prevents duplicate elements. When you try to add a duplicate element, the underlying HashMap's put() method detects that the key already exists and simply replaces the value (which is always PRESENT anyway), effectively doing nothing meaningful.

Key Points


  • HashSet internally creates: private transient HashMap<E, Object> map;
  • The dummy value: private static final Object PRESENT = new Object();
  • add(e) internally calls: map.put(e, PRESENT)
  • remove(e) internally calls: map.remove(e)
  • contains(e) internally calls: map.containsKey(e)

How Hashing Decides Where an Element Is Stored

Since HashSet is backed by a HashMap, adding an element isn't just "append it somewhere" - Java uses hashing to decide exactly where:

  • Hash Code - When an element is added, its hashCode() method is called to compute a hash code.
  • Bucket - That hash code is used to determine which bucket (a slot in the underlying HashMap's internal array) the element belongs to.
  • Collisions - Multiple elements can land in the same bucket if their hash codes collide; the bucket then holds multiple entries as a small linked list (or, for a heavily-loaded bucket, a balanced tree since Java 8).
  • Checking / Removing - contains() and remove() also compute the element's hash code first, jump straight to that bucket, and only then compare within that small bucket - this is why these operations are close to O(1) instead of scanning every element.

Every HashSet Method Is a Thin Wrapper Around a HashMap Method

Because HashSet has no logic of its own beyond delegation, you can read its entire public API as a one-to-one mapping onto HashMap:

HashSet MethodWhat It Actually Calls Internally
add(e)map.put(e, PRESENT) == null
remove(e)map.remove(e) == PRESENT
contains(e)map.containsKey(e)
size()map.size()
isEmpty()map.isEmpty()
clear()map.clear()
iterator()map.keySet().iterator()

Memory cost this implies: every element you add to a HashSet doesn't just cost the element itself - it costs a full HashMap Node (key reference + the shared PRESENT value reference + hash int + next pointer). This is why a HashSet always uses noticeably more memory per element than a plain array or ArrayList would.

LinkedHashSet variant: LinkedHashSet follows the exact same delegation pattern, except its internal field is a LinkedHashMap instead of a plain HashMap - that's the only difference, and it's why LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order.

Internal Working of HashSet - How add() Returns false for Duplicates

When you pass a duplicate element in Set, the add() method returns false. The main question is HOW it returns false.

When you open the HashSet implementation of the add() method in Java API, you find:

public class HashSet<E> extends AbstractSet<E> implements Set<E>, Cloneable, java.io.Serializable {
    private transient HashMap<E, Object> map;
    /* dummy value associated with object in map */
    private static final Object PRESENT = new Object();

    public HashSet() {
        map = new HashMap<>();
    }

    public boolean add(E e) {
        return map.put(e, PRESENT) == null;
    }
}

Key Observations:


  • We achieve uniqueness in Set internally through HashMap.
  • When you create an object of HashSet, it creates an object of HashMap internally.
  • What we do in Set is pass an argument in add(Element E) - that E becomes the key in HashMap, and some dummy value (new Object()) referred by PRESENT is passed as the value.
  • When you do hashset.add(3), Java internally does map.put(3, PRESENT).

The Main Point - map.put(key, value) returns:


1. null - if the key is unique and added to the map.
2. Old value of key - if the key is a duplicate.

So in HashSet add() method:

  • If map.put(e, PRESENT) returns null then map.put(e, PRESENT) == null returns TRUE - element added.
  • If map.put(e, PRESENT) returns old value then map.put(e, PRESENT) == null returns FALSE - element NOT added (duplicate).

Hashing Mechanism in HashSet

Since HashSet is backed by HashMap, the hashing mechanism determines how elements are stored and retrieved.

How Elements Are Stored and Retrieved:


  • Each element's hashCode() is computed.
  • The hash code determines the bucket location in HashMap.
  • HashMap consists of an array of buckets.
  • Each bucket holds multiple entries with the same hash code (collisions handled using linked list or balanced tree).

Operations:


  • Adding: Compute hash -> check bucket -> if not present, add as key with PRESENT value.
  • Removing: Compute hash -> remove corresponding key from HashMap.
  • Checking containment: Compute hash -> check bucket for key.

Seeing a Real Collision Happen

To actually witness bucket collisions rather than just read about them, force two different objects to share the same hashCode() - HashSet still keeps both, because equals() (not hashCode()) is what decides if two elements are "the same."

Class Diagram: HashSet's Inheritance vs Composition

Two different UML relationships are at play here, and mixing them up is a common misconception. HashSet extends AbstractSet (inheritance, an "is-a" relationship) but contains a HashMap (composition, a "has-a" relationship) - it does NOT extend HashMap.

AbstractCollection<E>
△ extends
AbstractSet<E>   implements Set<E>
△ extends
HashSet<E>  implements Set<E>, Cloneable, Serializable
- map: HashMap<E, Object>
◆ composes (has-a, NOT extends)
HashMap<E, Object>

LinkedHashSet slots in as a subclass of HashSet (extends HashSet<E>) that swaps the private map field's runtime type to a LinkedHashMap instead of a plain HashMap - same composition pattern, one field-type change, and insertion order comes along for free.

Why this distinction matters: because it's composition, HashSet's own methods are hand-written one-line delegations (add(e) { return map.put(e, PRESENT) == null; }) rather than inherited HashMap behavior - if HashSet extended HashMap directly, it would inherit HashMap's put(K,V)/get(K) two-argument key-value methods too, which makes no sense for a single-element Set API.

Memory Diagram: What add() Actually Builds on the Heap

The class diagram showed the type relationships; this shows what physically gets allocated when you call set.add("Java") on an empty HashSet.

HEAP

table[16] → bucket array
table[index] → Node@N1
hash = 2314539 (from "Java".hashCode(), bit-spread)
key → String@"Java"
value → PRESENT@shared
next → null
Add a second element set.add("Python") that happens to land in the SAME bucket:
table[index] → Node@N2 {key→"Python", value→PRESENT@shared, next → Node@N1}

Two details this diagram makes concrete:
1. Only ONE PRESENT object ever exists for the entire HashSet's lifetime - every single Node's value field points to that same shared instance. Adding a millionth element doesn't allocate a millionth dummy value; it reuses the one from HashSet's construction.
2. When a second element collides into the same bucket, the new Node doesn't replace the old one - since Java 8 it is APPENDED AT THE TAIL of that bucket's list (head insertion was the Java 7 behaviour, changed to avoid the resize infinite-loop bug), with next pointing back to the previous occupant, forming the linked list one node at a time as elements arrive.

Fresher Notes

  • A HashSet is implemented with a HashMap: each element is a key and a shared constant PRESENT object is the value.
  • add(e) is map.put(e, PRESENT) == null, which is why add returns false for duplicates.
  • So HashSet has the same performance as the HashMap behind it.

Internal Working of HashMap

HashMap stores key-value pairs and uses hashing for efficient retrieval, insertion, and deletion operations.

Key Concepts


  • Hashing: The process of converting a key into an integer (hash code) using the key's hashCode() method. This hash code is used to determine where the entry is stored.

  • Buckets: HashMap internally uses an array called the bucket array (or table). Each index in this array is a "bucket" that can hold one or more entries. The default array size is 16.

  • Node Structure: Each entry in HashMap is stored as a Node (inner class) containing:
  - key - The key of the entry.
  - value - The value associated with the key.
  - hash - The computed hash code of the key.
  - next - A reference (pointer) to the next Node in the same bucket (for handling collisions via linked list).

The Node Class (Simplified)


FieldTypePurpose
hashintPre-computed, bit-spread hash code of the key
keyKThe actual key object
valueVThe actual value object
nextNode<K,V>Link to the next Node in the same bucket (null if last)

HashMap Put, Get, and Remove Operations


1. Put Operation (Insertion):


  • The put method calculates the hash code of the key and determines the bucket index.
  • If the bucket is empty, the new key-value pair is placed in that bucket.
  • If the bucket already has nodes, the key is compared with existing keys using the equals method.
  • If a match is found, the value is updated.
  • If no match is found, a new node is added (linked list or tree node).

2. Get Operation (Retrieval):


  • The get method calculates the hash code of the key to determine the bucket.
  • Searches the bucket for a matching key using the equals method.
  • If found, returns the associated value.
  • If not found, returns null.

3. Remove Operation:


  • Calculates the hash code to find the bucket.
  • Searches for the key in the bucket.
  • If found, removes the node and returns the value.

Treeification, Resize, and Performance


1. Treeification - the Full Rule (Not Just "8 Nodes"):


Most explanations stop at "8 nodes triggers a tree," which is actually incomplete and misleading. The real rule has a second condition:

ConstantValueMeaning
TREEIFY_THRESHOLD8A bucket with 8+ nodes is a candidate for treeification
MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY64The tree conversion only actually happens if the WHOLE table has ≥ 64 buckets
UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD6A tree shrinks back to a linked list once it drops to 6 or fewer nodes

Why this matters: if a bucket hits 8 nodes while the table is still small (say, capacity 16), HashMap does NOT build a tree yet - it just resizes the table instead (more buckets means the 8 colliding keys likely spread out across different buckets on rehash). Only once the table has grown to at least 64 buckets AND a bucket still has 8+ nodes does the actual Red-Black tree conversion happen. This two-step guard avoids the overhead of building tiny trees on a small, still-growing table.

2. Resize/Rehashing:


  • When total entries exceed capacity * loadFactor, HashMap doubles its capacity.
  • Default: capacity 16, loadFactor 0.75, so resize at 12 entries.
  • All existing entries are rehashed and redistributed to new buckets.
  • This is an expensive operation but necessary to maintain O(1) average performance.

Capacity Growth Table (Default Load Factor 0.75)


CapacityResize Threshold (capacity × 0.75)
16 (default)12
3224
6448
12896
256192

3. Node Structure:


  • Each entry is a Node containing: key, value, hash code, reference to next node.

4. Performance:


  • Average case: O(1) for get, put, remove.
  • Worst case: O(log n) with tree (Java 8+), O(n) before Java 8.
  • Space complexity: O(n).

How hashCode() and equals() Actually Compute the Bucket Index


HashMap does not use the raw hash code as-is. Internally, it takes 3 steps:

1. Compute hash code: int hashCode = key.hashCode();
2. Spread the bits (Java 8+): int hash = hashCode ^ (hashCode >>> 16); - XORs the high 16 bits into the low 16 bits, so keys don't collide just because their low bits happen to match. This step alone is why Java 8's HashMap has far fewer collisions than pre-8 versions.
3. Calculate the bucket index: int index = (n - 1) & hash; - a fast bitwise AND instead of the slower % modulo, which only works correctly because the bucket array size n is always kept a power of two.

Collision resolution then relies on equals(): if two keys land in the same bucket (same index), HashMap walks the bucket's linked list (or tree) and calls equals() on each existing key to find an exact match. If equals() returns true, the value is replaced; otherwise a new node is appended.

Golden rule: if you override equals() on a class you plan to use as a HashMap key, you MUST also override hashCode() consistently (equal objects must produce equal hash codes) - otherwise two "equal" keys can land in different buckets and both get stored, silently breaking the map.

Seeing a Real Bucket Collision Happen

Same idea as the HashSet collision demo, but for HashMap directly: force two different keys to hash into the same bucket and watch HashMap fall back to equals() to tell them apart, keeping both as separate entries in that bucket's linked list.

Class Diagram: HashMap's Structure and Its Node Hierarchy

Unlike HashSet (which composes a whole separate HashMap object), HashMap doesn't delegate to anything - it IS the bottom of the delegation chain. What's interesting here instead is the internal Node class hierarchy that most explanations skip over.

The surprising part: HashMap's own TreeNode (used for the treeified Red-Black tree buckets) doesn't extend Node directly - it extends LinkedHashMap.Entry, which itself extends Node. HashMap reaches into LinkedHashMap's inner class purely to inherit the before/after pointer fields, even though a plain HashMap never uses them for ordering - it's just convenient field reuse across the two classes, a detail that only shows up by reading the actual JDK source.

Memory Diagram: What put() Actually Builds on the Heap

Same style as HashSet's diagram, but now the Node holds a real value instead of the shared PRESENT dummy - and this time there's a second diagram worth seeing: what a resize actually does to existing Nodes.

HEAP - after map.put("Pankaj", 90000)

What Resize Actually Does to Existing Nodes (Not a Full Rehash!)

When capacity doubles from 16 to 32, most explanations say "everything gets rehashed" - but Java 8+ HashMap is smarter than that. Since capacity is always a power of 2, doubling it only adds one new bit to the index calculation. So instead of recomputing each Node's hash from scratch, resize just checks that one extra bit and splits each old bucket's list into exactly two groups: lo (bit is 0 - stays at the same index) and hi (bit is 1 - moves to oldIndex + oldCapacity).

Resize from capacity 16 to 32 - old bucket table[9] had 2 nodes
new table[9] (lo group - extra bit was 0)
Node@N1 {key="Pankaj", ...} - the SAME object, just relinked, not recreated 		new table[25] (hi group - extra bit was 1, 9+16=25)
Node@N2 {key="Dheeraj", ...} - the SAME object, relinked here instead

The key insight: resize is cheaper than it sounds - it's an array-splitting operation that reuses the exact same Node objects (no new Node allocations, no hashCode() recomputation), just relinking each one's next pointer into one of two new chains. This is specifically a Java 8 optimization; pre-Java-8 HashMap really did recompute everything on resize.

Fresher Notes

  • HashMap uses an array of buckets (Node<K,V>[] table); each node holds hash, key, value and next.
  • put: compute hash, find index (n-1) & hash, then add to the bucket or update the existing key.
  • get: same index, then compare the hash and equals through the bucket.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Mid-Level Notes

  • Collisions form a linked list; since Java 8 a bucket with 8 or more nodes (and table size at least 64) becomes a red-black tree.
  • The table resizes (doubles) when size exceeds capacity times load factor (0.75), redistributing nodes.
  • The hash spreads high bits: h ^ (h >>> 16).

Senior Notes

  • Capacity is always a power of two so the index is a cheap bit mask.
  • Treeified bins use compareTo when keys are Comparable, giving O(log n) worst case.
  • Concurrent modification (races) can corrupt a HashMap; ConcurrentHashMap uses CAS and per-bin synchronization.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Cost model: a lookup is hash computation, one array access, and a short chain compare, so keys with expensive hashCode or equals dominate. Cache a hash (String does), keep keys small and immutable, and avoid resizing by pre-sizing.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: debugging a slow lookup. A bad hashCode (such as returning a constant, or only the first field) causes one huge bucket; fix with a hash over all identity fields.
